reasoning: Dalton was the first to use symbols to stand for the elements, each symbol also denoting a definite quantity — one atom — of that element. The one- and two-letter notation actually in use today (H, O, Na) is the later proposal of Berzelius, so a reader taking 'symbol of element' to mean the modern symbol would answer Berzelius instead; the stem does not say which it means. Dalton is taken as the answer because the stem's verb is 'introduced', i.e. first used, which is how the standard Class 9 treatment words Dalton's contribution while crediting Berzelius separately with the letter form.
basis: The only disagreement in the paper, and BOTH passes rated it LOW and independently identified the SAME fork — Dalton first to use symbols, Berzelius the modern letter system — rather than one simply being wrong. Neither reading is a mistake; the stem is defective in that it omits the one word ('modern', or 'first') that would decide it. Adjudicated to Dalton on TWO grounds. First, the verb: 'introduced' reads as priority, and the standard Class 9 source these papers draw on says in as many words that Dalton was the first to use symbols for elements, crediting Berzelius separately with making symbols from one or two letters of the name. Second, and independent of any source, the DISTRACTOR SET points the same way: Boyle (1660s) and Lavoisier (1780s) are both PRE-Dalton, so the axis the question discriminates on is chronological priority among early chemists — a set built around the modern notation would more naturally offer nineteenth-century contemporaries of Berzelius. No official key exists for this paper and neither reading can be confirmed; a student answering Berzelius is not wrong, and the stored solution says so.
